This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.


Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The task came from the parent session (local_3e38de32-e8df-4f8c-b26d-1a20db4c0aca). Find out why the first batch of the JusPrin 2 launch email has a low open rate, and fix it before Kenneth sends to more people. No further batch goes out until Kenneth says so.

   The batch was sent through SendGrid Marketing Campaigns LEGACY:
   - Campaign 22621835, sent 6:51 AM PST Nov 13, 2026.
   - Sender: "Kenneth from JusPrin" <jusprin-support@obico.io>.
   - Subject: "JusPrin 2: open source AI slicer, free with your own API key".
   - Recipients: segment 14021983, the 310 free JusPrin 1 users who chatted in the last 30 days.
   - Unsubscribe group: The Spaghetti Detective (id 8150).

   Steps the task asked for:
   1. Re-read batch 1's numbers and compare them with earlier campaigns (33–57% opens), watching how opens grow over 24–48 hours.
   2. Check Postmaster Tools for Nov 13–14.
   3. Design and run small test sends that tell the causes apart: Gmail's Promotions tab, the SpamCop-listed shared IP, one-click unsubscribe, English to a mostly Brazilian audience, few Apple Mail users, the subject line. Propose a fix for each confirmed cause, with its cost.
   4. Ask Kenneth before sending to real recipients, spending money, or deleting anything in SendGrid. Never click "Send Campaign" on draft 22624323, which still has the 310-person segment.

   Done means a short report to Kenneth, under 500 words in plain sentences: the cause, the evidence, the recommended change for batch 2, and what's unverified.

   Kenneth later chose "Free GlockApps test" and signed in to GlockApps.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - SendGrid Marketing Campaigns LEGACY UI is at sendgrid.com/marketing_campaigns/ui/campaigns. Stats are at /marketing_campaigns/campaigns/{id}/stats, with a stats.csv export.
   - The SendGrid v3 API works from the signed-in page with fetch and credentials:'include'. Used: /v3/campaigns, /v3/contactdb/lists, /v3/contactdb/recipients, /v3/campaigns/{id}/schedules/now, /v3/senders, /v3/mailbox_providers/stats, /v3/suppression/{bounces,blocks,...}.
   - Google Postmaster Tools v2 (compliance, spam, delivery errors). The v1 domain-reputation dashboards are gone.
   - GlockApps manual seed test: a test ID string goes in the email body, then the email is sent to 131 seed addresses. Placements come back by provider.
   - Gmail tabs (Promotions vs Primary), sender identity reputation, and one-click List-Unsubscribe (RFC 8058).
   - Production Django shell through /Users/kenneth/Projects/ops/tsd/prod/run_django_mgmt_cmd.sh, read only.
   - gog CLI for k@obico.io Gmail, read only, run outside the sandbox.

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - Parent session scratchpad (personal data, chmod 600, never commit or upload): `/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/8455462d-9c30-4fdc-8b53-80de35da8f7a/scratchpad/wave/`
     - batch1_emails.txt holds 310 addresses. Its order matches batch1_ids.txt, which is one comma-separated line of 310 Obico user ids.
     - Also there: campaign.html, campaign_plain.html, send.py, ids.py, list.py, export.py, test_full.json.
   - My scratchpad: `/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/8753b55f-488a-41c6-8e05-2221784a21f3/scratchpad/`
     - age.py and age.out: sign-up date and chat stats per recipient id.
     - v2.py and v2.out: JusPrin 2 accounts per recipient.
     - test912.json and test912.eml: the raw 6:31 AM test email.
     - seeds.txt, seeds_list.txt and seeds.csv: the 131 GlockApps seeds, list hash 84b11fd62c1149f6.
   - Shared note, holding all evidence and test results: `/Users/kenneth/Library/Application Support/Claude/side-session-notes/local_3e38de32-e8df-4f8c-b26d-1a20db4c0aca/jusprin2-batch1-low-opens.md`
   - SendGrid objects I created:
     - List 32183815 "GlockApps seeds - TEST ONLY 2026-11-13" with 130 seed contacts. One of the 131 seeds didn't persist.
     - Campaign 22624422 "TEST A - GlockApps seeds only - batch 1 as sent (jusprin-support@)". Sender 10028875; ID id:2026-11-13-17:48:52:293t in a 10px grey footer line inserted before </body> at index 2970, and appended to the plain text. Sent 17:51 UTC.
     - Campaign 22624426 "TEST B …" with sender 3626841 "Obi The Owl" <support@obico.io>, the same content, and ID id:2026-11-13-17:51:57:086t. Sent 17:52 UTC.
   - GlockApps reports:
     - https://app.glockapps.com/inbox-insight/spam-tests/reports/2026-11-13-17:48:52:293t/deliverability
     - https://app.glockapps.com/inbox-insight/spam-tests/reports/2026-11-13-17:51:57:086t/deliverability

4. Errors and fixes:
   - mc.sendgrid.com/campaigns returned 404. The legacy URLs are on sendgrid.com/marketing_campaigns/.
   - A cross-origin fetch from the Postmaster tab failed, so I navigated to a SendGrid page first.
   - The Chrome output filter returned "[BLOCKED: Cookie/query string data]" on outputs containing URLs or query strings. I stripped URLs, or read only booleans and counts.
   - In zsh, `echo ======` gave "not found". I used other separators.
   - The legacy contact DB count lagged (64, then 130), so I waited and re-checked before sending.
   - Navigating tab 268837466 was blocked by GlockApps' "Leave site?" dialog. I used tab 268837476 instead. Closing 268837466 timed out; it may still be open, waiting on that dialog.

5. Problem Solving and Findings:
   - **Open rates:** Gmail recipients opened batch 1 at 7.5%. In mailbox-provider stats, Gmail recipients opened earlier campaigns at 42–47%.
   - **End-of-first-day opens for earlier campaigns:**

     | Campaign | End of first day | Final |
     |---|---|---|
     | JusPrin 1.4.0 | 26.1% | 41.6% |
     | Next-Gen AI b2 | 33.8% | not recorded |
     | JusPrin 1.1.0, non-English users | 37.5% | 65.4% |
     | JusPrin 1.3.0 | 11.1% | 33.2% |
     | JusPrin public release b1 | 30.5% | 47.8% |
     | Re-Inventing TSD b1 | 16.6% | 55.7% |

   - **Sender history:** every earlier campaign used "Obi The Owl" <support@obico.io>. The jusprin-support senders were created only days ago.
   - **Ruled out:**
     - Apple Mail auto-opens: the drop is inside Gmail.
     - Language: the English-subject email to non-English users got 65%.
     - Audience quality: flat opens across account age and activity.
     - Gmail rejections over sender requirements: none in the bounces.
     - One-click unsubscribe on this email: the headers are present. Postmaster's "needs work" covers obico.io's other mail, which obico-server PR 1176 fixes.
     - SpamCop: it lists only one SendGrid IP.
   - **GlockApps result (read about 10:05 AM PST):**

     | Seeds | Copy A (current sender) | Copy B (Obi The Owl, support@) |
     |---|---|---|
     | Overall | Inbox 43.8%, Tabs 23.1%, Spam 23.1%, Missing 10% | Inbox 59.2%, Tabs 5.4%, Spam 19.2%, Missing 16.2% |
     | Gmail (22) | Promotions 22 | Primary 22 |
     | Yahoo (8) | Spam 7, Inbox 1 | Inbox 8 |
     | AOL (8) | Spam 8 | Inbox 7, Missing 1 |
     | Hotmail (5) | Spam 3, Missing 2 | Spam 3, Missing 2 |
     | Outlook (8) | Spam 2, Missing 6 | Spam 2, Missing 6 |
     | iCloud (3) | Missing 3 | Missing 3 |

     The content filters passed for copy A: Google "Not spam", SpamAssassin 3.5.
   - **Caveats:**
     - Copy B changes both the display name and the address, so the test can't say which matters.
     - "Missing" results may still update.
     - Microsoft and iCloud placement is a separate problem that the sender change doesn't fix.
   - **Scheduled re-checks (session-only crons):** ff350090 at 9:07 PM Nov 13, and afaccbe1 at 7:13 AM Nov 14. Both re-read the open curve and Postmaster Tools and append to the note.
   - **Costs gathered:** GlockApps free plan has 2 tests, both now used. Paid plans are about $59+/month, though sources conflict. A dedicated IP needs a paid SendGrid plan plus weeks of warm-up.

6. All user messages:
   - The initial task from the parent session, with these constraints verbatim: "Ask Kenneth before: sending anything to real recipients; spending money, such as a seed-list service like GlockApps or a dedicated IP; deleting anything in SendGrid. Draft campaign 22624323 is a copy made for test sends, and it still has the 310-person batch 1 segment as its recipients. Never click 'Send Campaign' on it." Also: the recipient files "(chmod 600, contain personal data, never commit or upload)". Also: "No further batch goes out until Kenneth says so." Also: "In SendGrid campaign rows, a delete icon sits right next to the duplicate icon. Click by element, not by coordinates." Also: use the gcloud account ai-agent@tsdtechnology.iam.gserviceaccount.com, read-only production.
   - "Free GlockApps test" (Kenneth's answer to which test to run).
   - "Signed in" (Kenneth signed in to GlockApps).

7. Pending Tasks:
   - Write the closing message, the final report to Kenneth. wrap_up was already called with the question "Which sender should batch 2 use?" and two buttons, so don't repeat that question in the text.
   - Wait for Kenneth's choice of sender for batch 2. Don't send batch 2 without his explicit go-ahead.
   - Let the scheduled crons run (9:07 PM tonight, 7:13 AM tomorrow) to watch the open curve and Postmaster Nov 13 data.
   - Later cleanup, but only with Kenneth's OK before deleting: SendGrid list 32183815 and its seed contacts, and campaigns 22624422 and 22624426.
   - GlockApps tab 268837466 may still be stuck on a "Leave site?" dialog in Kenneth's Chrome.

8. Current Work:
   I had just finished the GlockApps seed test and appended its results to the shared note. I closed tab 268837476 and called wrap_up. Its recap: "The seed test shows the new sender address caused the low opens. From jusprin-support@obico.io, all 22 Gmail test inboxes put batch 1 in Promotions. From support@obico.io, the same email landed in Primary in all 22. Nothing went to real recipients, and batch 2 is still on hold." Its ask: "Which sender should batch 2 use?" Its buttons: "Obi The Owl, support@" and "Kenneth from JusPrin, support@". The tool flagged the second label as too long. The closing message hadn't been written yet.

9. Optional Next Step:
   Write the closing report to Kenneth in plain sentences, under about 500 words:
   - **Cause:** the new sender address, shown by Gmail seeds landing in Promotions (22/22) versus Primary (22/22) with support@obico.io. Yahoo and AOL moved from Spam to Inbox.
   - **Evidence:** the 7.5% vs 42–47% Gmail open rates, the flat cohort result, and the ruled-out causes.
   - **Recommendation for batch 2:** send from support@obico.io. Optionally consider re-sending to batch 1 non-openers, marked as a proposal that needs his OK.
   - **Unverified:** whether the display name or the address matters; the Microsoft and iCloud placement; the 24–48 hour open curve and Postmaster Nov 13 data, which the crons will pick up.
   - **Cleanup:** the SendGrid test objects, to be deleted only with his OK.
   - **Chrome:** the GlockApps tab may be waiting on a "Leave site?" dialog.
   - **Sources:** include the GlockApps pricing sources cited earlier.

If you need specific details from before compaction (like exact code snippets, error messages, or content you generated), read the full transcript at: /Users/kenneth/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/8753b55f-488a-41c6-8e05-2221784a21f3.jsonl

The messages after this summary are the most recent messages from before compaction, kept verbatim. The summary was written without seeing them, so something it says has not happened yet may already have happened in them.

The seed test points to the sender address. The same batch 1 email went to 131 GlockApps test inboxes twice:
- **Copy A**, from "Kenneth from JusPrin" <jusprin-support@obico.io>: all 22 Gmail inboxes filed it in Promotions.
- **Copy B**, from "Obi The Owl" <support@obico.io>, the sender every earlier campaign used: all 22 Gmail inboxes put it in Primary.

That fits the open rates: Gmail users opened earlier campaigns at 42–47% and batch 1 at 7.5%. No real recipients got anything.

**Results by provider** (number of test inboxes in brackets):

| Provider | From jusprin-support@obico.io | From support@obico.io |
|---|---|---|
| Gmail (22) | Promotions: 22 | Primary: 22 |
| Yahoo (8) | Spam: 7, inbox: 1 | Inbox: 8 |
| AOL (8) | Spam: 8 | Inbox: 7, not received: 1 |
| Hotmail and Outlook (13) | Spam: 5, not received: 8 | Same |
| iCloud (3) | Not received: 3 | Same |
| Google Workspace (5) | Inbox: 5 | Same |

- Google's and Microsoft's content filters both rated copy A "not spam", so the wording and the links aren't the problem.
- In batch 1, 202 of the 310 recipients were at Gmail or Yahoo, so this one change affects about two-thirds of the list.
- Hotmail and Outlook filed both copies in Spam or didn't receive them. That's a separate problem that the sender change doesn't fix. It covers about 31 recipients per batch, and I haven't looked into its cause.
- These numbers are from about 13 minutes after sending. Some "not received" counts may still change.

**What isn't proven:** copy B changed both the display name and the address. I can't tell whether "Kenneth from JusPrin" with support@obico.io would also reach Primary. Both free GlockApps tests are used up, and another test would need a paid plan, which third-party reviews put at about $59 a month and up.

**Recommendation for batch 2:** send from "Obi The Owl" <support@obico.io>, the only sender proven to reach Primary. The other choice is a new SendGrid sender, "Kenneth from JusPrin" <support@obico.io>, which would need verifying in SendGrid before it can send. It sounds more personal, but it's untested.

**Batch 1 recipients:** you could re-send to the 289 people who haven't opened, from support@obico.io. That's a separate decision for later.

**Things left in SendGrid and Chrome:**
- In SendGrid: a list named "GlockApps seeds - TEST ONLY 2026-11-13" with the 130 test addresses, and two sent test campaigns, 22624422 and 22624426. I'll delete them only when you say.
- A GlockApps tab is still open in Chrome and may be showing a "Leave site?" box. Clicking Leave is safe: both tests are finished.

**Still scheduled:** re-checks of batch 1's open curve and Postmaster Tools at 9 PM tonight and 7 AM tomorrow, while this session stays open.

The full results are in `jusprin2-batch1-low-opens.md` in the shared notes folder.
Obi The Owl, support@

Gmail tends to be cautious with first-time senders and recipients, so a low open rate on a first email to new contacts is common and usually points to deliverability rather than copy.

- **Sender reputation and engagement history:** New domains and IPs have no track record, so initial emails to new recipients often go to spam. Gmail relies heavily on user engagement to determine inbox placement.
- **Authentication:** Insufficient SPF, DKIM, or DMARC setup is listed as a contributing factor for first emails landing in spam (source 4-3).
- **List quality:** Emails sent to invalid addresses bounce, and a bounce rate above 2% signals to email providers that you're not maintaining a clean list.
- **Diagnostics:** Check Gmail Postmaster Tools for domain reputation, and run a seed test across Gmail, Outlook, and Yahoo to see inbox versus spam placement directly (sources 13-3 to 13-5).
- **Ramp-up:** One guide suggests a staged schedule, starting with about 5 sends per day per inbox to engaged contacts only and building volume over several weeks (source 16-1).
- **Engagement tactics:** Asking recipients to add you to their contacts or reply can signal positive engagement to Gmail (source 4-6).

Sources disagree on emphasis. Some vendor guides push subject lines first, while deliverability-focused sources argue that deliverability operations, not copywriting tricks, determine whether your cold outbound campaigns succeed. Most of these are vendor blogs, so treat their specific benchmarks as directional.

input.prompt: What exactly changed in Gmail open tracking, when (dates), how large, and what evidence? Does it affect all senders or only some (e.g. new vs engaged recipients, Promotions)?

result.output:
**What changed and when**

- **Late November 2025:** Gmail image loading, including tracking pixels, dropped by roughly one third, according to Validity's engagement data. The article attributes this to Gmail possibly reducing image prefetching through its proxy servers, but calls this an industry speculation.
- **Late 2025:** Gmail moved from soft enforcement of non-compliant bulk mail to actively rejecting it with hard SMTP-level codes. Rejected messages generate no opens.
- **Late 2025:** Gmail began sorting the Promotions tab by engagement rather than recency. The article gives no exact date.
- **Late 2025:** A Purchases tab was introduced. The article gives no exact date for the tab's rollout, and the author says some marketing emails have landed there.
- **Mid-2025:** Subscriptions Manager launched and was later rolled out to personal accounts. Users can unsubscribe from a sender in one click without opening email.
- **January 2026:** AI-generated summaries and Gemini inbox search began rolling out. These affect how users read and search email, but the article is unsure whether summaries inflate opens.

**Size and evidence**

- Some Validity customers saw quarter-over-quarter open rate drops of 30% or more.
- Gmail inbox placement fell about 3%, according to the Validity Intelligence Network.
- The article's evidence is Validity's own aggregate data, customer reports, and the author's analysis. It does not give a formal breakdown of the open rate decline by cause.

**Who is affected**

- **Not all senders equally.** The article says Promotions sorting and Gemini search disproportionately affect low-engagement senders and recipients, since less engaged mail is pushed down and less human interaction occurs.
- **Engaged senders are less affected.** The article says senders aren't seeing similar declines in clicks and revenue, which suggests the drop is mostly from fewer false opens rather than fewer readers.
- **Specific senders are affected by specific features.** Message clipping affects any sender whose HTML exceeds about 1KB. Purchases tab routing affects marketing emails with delivery-policy content. Subscriptions Manager affects high-frequency senders, and list shrinkage from it may be a net positive.
- **Address changes and inactive accounts** reduce opens from specific addresses regardless of engagement strategy.
- **The article doesn't compare new versus engaged recipients** in quantitative terms, so that distinction is only inferred from the engagement-based mechanisms it describes.

content.text:
The new sender address explains part of the low open rate, now measured on real recipients. 16 hours after sending, batch 2 from support@obico.io had been opened by 22.6% of recipients, compared with 14.3% for batch 1 from jusprin-support@obico.io. That's the same email and the same point in time. My updated view is that the audience explains more of the gap with earlier campaigns than the sender does. That part is an inference, not proven.

**Current numbers, at 5:53 AM**

| | Batch 1 (jusprin-support@) | Batch 2 (support@) |
|---|---|---|
| Hours since sending | 23 | 16 |
| Unique opens | 44 of 301 (14.6%) | 45 of 199 (22.6%) |
| Gmail opens | 36 of 242 (14.9%) | 40 of 171 (23.4%) |
| Clicks | 1 | 2 |

Batch 1 gained one new opener overnight, so it has stopped growing at about 15%.

**Why I think the audience matters more**

Even from the sender that reaches Gmail's Primary tab, batch 2 is at 22.6%. Earlier campaigns from that same sender reached 33–56%. So the sender change alone doesn't close the gap.

I matched production data against who opened, with emails hashed inside the page. Of the 547 JusPrin 1 users who chatted since Sep 19, only 18 have ever had an Obico printer. That's 3%, so almost none of them get Obico's printer notification emails. They have little reason to recognise or open mail from obico.io.

- The 2026 campaigns that got 44–56% went to Obico printer users.
- The JusPrin 1.4.0 email in Oct 2025 got 41.6% from early JusPrin users. About a quarter of them had Obico printers.
- In batch 1, the 10 printer owners opened at 60% even from the new sender. Everyone else opened at 13%.
- That printer comparison rests on very few people. Batch 2's six printer owners opened 0 of 6.

Some outside context, from vendor blogs I can't verify: Validity reports that since late November 2025, Gmail loads about a third fewer images, which counts as fewer opens. Gmail also started sorting the Promotions tab by how much each person engages with the sender. Mail to Obico's printer users didn't visibly suffer from this in Feb and Apr 2026. People with no history with obico.io may be hit harder.

**One thing I checked and set aside:** almost all batch contacts were created in SendGrid on Nov 12. That looked like proof they'd never been emailed. But 35,000 of the 47,000 contacts on the TSD list were also created that day, and old open history is gone, so contacts were deleted and re-added at some point. It tells us nothing about these people.

**Still unproven:** the audience explanation rests on a small printer-owner sample. There's no recent campaign from support@ to non-Obico users to compare against. Clicks are too few to compare: 1 and 2.

Everything is in `jusprin2-batch1-low-opens.md` in the shared notes folder. The 7:13 and 7:17 AM checks will add one more reading of each batch.

Sources:
- [Validity: what's really behind Gmail's open rate drop](https://www.validity.com/blog/whats-really-behind-gmails-open-rate-drop-and-what-to-do-about-it/)
- [Klaviyo community: declining Gmail open rates 2026](https://community.klaviyo.com/analytics-72/declining-gmail-open-rates-2026-19952)
- [Suped: low open rates for new Gmail signups](https://suped.com/email-deliverability/answers/why-do-new-gmail-signups-or-new-email-templates-have-low-open-rates)
Any hypothesis remaining? and what experiment we should run next to validate those hypotheses?

Two explanations are measured: the new sender address, and Gmail's Promotions tab. Four are still open. For each one, here is the test I'd run next. None of these tests has been run yet.

**1. People with no history with obico.io open less, wherever the email lands.** This is my main remaining explanation. Only 3% of these recipients have ever had an Obico printer. Too few printer owners remain to test that directly. A comparison that should work: the SendGrid list still holds about 11,400 contacts created in Feb 2026. Those are probably the people who got the "Re-Inventing The Spaghetti Detective" email that month, though I haven't confirmed it. The test: send batch 3 from support@obico.io at one time. Then compare opens between batch 3 recipients who are among those Feb 2026 contacts and those who aren't. It costs nothing. It works only if enough remaining JusPrin 1 users are in the Feb 2026 group, which I'd count first.

**2. Opens are undercounting people who actually read the email.** Gmail has been loading fewer tracking images since late 2025. The better measure is whether recipients went on to make a JusPrin 2 account. A read-only production query can count that for batch 1, batch 2, and similar JusPrin 1 users who weren't emailed. It's free, and it tells us whether the email works even where opens look low.

**3. The subject line.** "JusPrin 2: open source AI slicer, free with your own API key" may read as an ad. SendGrid's legacy campaigns have no A/B testing, so the test would mean splitting one batch in half by hand, with two subjects. Each half needs about 300 people to tell 20% from 30% reliably. That only works once batches are a few hundred or larger.

**4. Send time.** Batch 1 went out at 6:51 AM Pacific, and batch 2 at 1:45 PM. If most recipients are in Brazil, that's late morning versus evening there. The effect is probably small. Keep the send time fixed in batch 3 so it doesn't muddy the other comparison.

Separately, Hotmail and Outlook put the seed-test copies in Spam or never delivered them, whichever sender we used. That covers about 10% of each batch. Testing it needs a paid GlockApps plan (about $59 a month in third-party reviews) or a few real Outlook inboxes. It's a separate problem from the Gmail one.

**Decision needed: what should batch 3 test?**

- **Opens by Obico history (my pick):** send all of batch 3 from support@obico.io at a single time, then compare opens between people with and without the Feb 2026 contact history. It costs nothing, but it depends on that group being big enough.
- **Subject lines:** split batch 3 into two halves with different subjects. That needs a batch of 600 or more to give a clear answer, and it adds work in SendGrid.
- **Nothing extra:** send batch 3 like batch 2. It costs nothing and teaches nothing new.

In any case, the JusPrin 2 sign-up count is cheap, and I can run it now. Which should batch 3 test?

input.ask: Should batch 3 be the 2,400-person test of subject and sender name?

content.text:
Yes. One batch can test the subject line and the sender name, and also show whether people's history with Obico matters. About 6,000 JusPrin 1 users haven't been emailed yet, and 79% of them use Gmail. That's enough people to answer all of this in one send.

**First, a correction.** I proposed splitting people by whether SendGrid had held them as contacts since Feb 2026. Only 8 of the 6,000 qualify, so that split won't work. Production data gives a better one. About 1,000 of the 6,000 have an Obico printer, so they already get mail from obico.io. About 3,900 started using JusPrin before mid-October 2025, so they were probably on the list for the JusPrin 1.3.0 and 1.4.0 emails. I haven't checked who actually received those.

**The four explanations I think are most likely**

1. People with no history with obico.io open less. This is my strongest suspect.
2. The display name "Obi The Owl" versus a person's name. The address (support@obico.io) is already settled. The name isn't tested.
3. The subject line. "Free with your own API key" may read as an ad, and "API key" may mean nothing to many users.
4. Opens are undercounting real readers. Gmail loads fewer tracking images now, so opens may miss people who did read the email.

**Proposed experiment for batch 3 (not approved, nothing built)**

- **Who gets it:** about 2,400 randomly chosen people from the 6,000. That leaves about 3,600 to receive whichever version wins.
- **Same for everyone:** sent from support@obico.io, all at the same minute.
- **Split by subject:** half get the current subject. The other half get a plainer one, such as "JusPrin 2 is here". You'd choose the exact wording.
- **Split by sender name:** independently, half see "Obi The Owl" and half see "Kenneth from JusPrin". So there are four combinations, with about 600 people each.
- **Balanced history:** the split is drawn so that printer owners, early JusPrin users and newer users are spread evenly across all four combinations.

What this answers:
- **Subject:** 1,200 people against 1,200. That's enough to see a gap of about 5 points.
- **Sender name:** the same comparison, using the other split.
- **History:** printer owners against everyone else, compared in all four combinations together. The cleanest comparison is among early users who last chatted in 2025: about 850 with printers and about 2,800 without. If my strongest suspect is right, printer owners should open roughly twice as often.
- **Undercounting:** I'd also count, from production, who creates a JusPrin 2 account within 7 days. If one subject wins on opens but not on sign-ups, the open counts are misleading.

Two tests are left out on purpose:
- **Send time:** held fixed so it doesn't muddy the rest.
- **Hotmail and Outlook spam:** a separate problem that affects about 10% of each batch.

Setting it up in SendGrid takes four segments built from a new field marking each person's version, plus four campaigns scheduled for the same minute. "Kenneth from JusPrin" sending from support@obico.io would be a new sender in SendGrid, and it has to be verified before it can send.

**Decision needed: how big should batch 3's test be?**

- **The full test above (my pick):** subject line and sender name together, about 2,400 people. It answers the most questions in one send. It needs one more SendGrid sender and four campaigns.
- **Subject line only:** about 1,200 people, everything sent as "Obi The Owl". Simpler to set up, but it says nothing about using your name.
- **Neither:** send everyone the batch 2 version. No new setup, but nothing new learned.

Which size do you want for batch 3?

input.ask: Should we spend about $59 on a GlockApps month to test SES against SendGrid on test inboxes?

content.text:
Yes. At the start I suspected SendGrid's shared sending servers, because SpamCop lists one of them as a spam source. The seed test since then shows SendGrid isn't the problem for Gmail, Yahoo or AOL. It's still a suspect for Hotmail, Outlook and iCloud. A split test with SES makes sense, but I'd run it on test inboxes first, not on real recipients.

**What the evidence shows**

The test copy from support@obico.io went through SendGrid's shared servers like everything else. It still landed in Gmail's Primary tab in all 22 Gmail inboxes. Yahoo had it in the inbox 8 of 8 times, and AOL 7 of 8. Whatever is wrong with SendGrid, it isn't hurting those providers.

Microsoft and Apple look different. Of 13 Hotmail and Outlook test inboxes, 5 put the email in Spam and 8 never received it. iCloud never received it in any of its 3. That held for both sender addresses, so it points at something shared by both copies: the sending servers, or the obico.io domain itself. Real recipients match this. Microsoft users opened 2 of 33 batch 1 emails and 1 of 18 batch 2 emails, and iCloud users opened 0 of 4. Those providers are about 12% of each batch. Even a full fix there would raise the overall open rate by only about 2 points.

**SES is already set up for obico.io**

Obico's server mail, such as the "We couldn't charge your Card" emails from admin@obico.io, already goes through Amazon SES. Gmail shows it passing both domain checks under obico.io's name. So a test send through SES needs no new DNS setup.

**Why not test it on real recipients yet**

- **Building:** SendGrid gives us the unsubscribe link, the one-click unsubscribe header, and open and click counts. SES gives us none of that ready-made. We'd have to build an unsubscribe that also updates SendGrid's unsubscribe group, plus open and click tracking.
- **Risk:** SES pauses a whole account if spam complaints pass 0.1% or bounces pass 5%. Batch 1 bounced 2.3%. A pause would also stop Obico's billing and alert emails, which share the same SES account.

**My proposal**

Repeat the seed test through both services: the same email from support@obico.io, sent once through SendGrid and once through SES, to the GlockApps test inboxes. If SES gets into Hotmail, Outlook and iCloud inboxes where SendGrid doesn't, a real-recipient split becomes worth the building work and the risk. If both fail the same way, the cause is the domain or the content, and switching services won't help.

**Decision needed:** our free GlockApps tests are used up. This one needs a paid month, which third-party reviews put at about $59, though sources disagree. The same month would also let us check the subject line and the "Kenneth from JusPrin" name on test inboxes before batch 3 goes to real people. The free alternative is a few real Outlook and iCloud inboxes that you or the team already own. That's cheaper, but those inboxes have history with you, so they're a weaker test. My pick is the paid month.
Not now

input.ask: Which wording should the second subject use?

content.text:
You're right: testing two things at once needs four groups. This is called a full factorial test, and it's the standard approach. With only two groups, say current subject with Obi The Owl and new subject with Kenneth, a winner wouldn't tell you whether the subject or the name made the difference.

With four groups, nothing is lost. Each comparison still uses everyone. Half the people see each subject, and that half is evenly split between the two names. So the subject comparison is 1,200 against 1,200, and the name comparison is too. You also get a rough hint of whether the name only helps with one subject. All four groups get batch 2's email from support@obico.io, sent at the same minute:

| Group | Subject | Sender name |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Current: "JusPrin 2: open source AI slicer, free with your own API key" | Obi The Owl |
| 2 | New subject | Obi The Owl |

- **Fair groups:** printer owners, early JusPrin users and Gmail users are spread evenly across the four groups. The assignment happens inside the SendGrid page, so no email addresses leave it.
- **What it can detect:** a difference of about 4–5 points in open rate, at the 12–20% rates we expect.
- **What I'll measure:** opens after 48 hours, clicks, and JusPrin 2 accounts created within 7 days.
- **How we pick winners, fixed before sending:** for each factor, the version with more opens wins only if the difference is statistically clear. If it isn't, there's no real difference and you choose. If opens and sign-ups disagree, sign-ups decide.
- **History question:** printer owners against everyone else is answered from all four groups together, at no extra cost.

**Building it once you approve:**

1. Mark each person's group in a new SendGrid contact field.
2. Add a "Kenneth from JusPrin" sender on support@obico.io. Your two jusprin-support@ senders were verified quickly, so I expect this one to be the same.

input.ask: Should batch 3 add send time as a third factor?

content.text:
Yes. The original list had nine possible causes. Batch 3 tests two of them by random split. It also answers two more without a split, because they can be read across all four groups. Three are already settled, and two are left out.

**Settled before batch 3**
- **Sender address:** jusprin-support@obico.io landed in Gmail's Promotions tab in the seed test, while support@obico.io landed in Primary. Real opens agree, so batch 3 uses support@obico.io for every group.
- **One-click unsubscribe:** the campaign email already has the header. Postmaster's warning is about Obico's own server mail.
- **Apple Mail opening emails automatically:** that would inflate opens, not lower them. The drop is inside Gmail, so it doesn't explain anything.

**Tested in batch 3 by random split**
- The subject line.
- The sender name, "Obi The Owl" or "Kenneth from JusPrin".

**Answered in batch 3 without a split**
- **History with obico.io:** we can't randomly give people an Obico printer, so this is read by comparing printer owners, early JusPrin users and newer users across all four groups. Each group gets an even share of each kind of person.
- **Opens undercounting real readers:** JusPrin 2 sign-ups within 7 days are counted alongside opens, so a subject that only wins on opens won't be picked.

**Left out**
- **Send time:** held at one minute for everyone, so it can't muddy the other results.
- **Language:** the email is in English. The idea that recipients are mostly Brazilian was never checked. A translated version needs the translation, plus a way to know each person's language, and we have neither.
- **SendGrid against Amazon SES:** you said not now.

Adding a third factor costs less than it sounds, because each comparison still uses everyone. With send time added, batch 3 becomes eight groups of about 300. The subject comparison is still 1,200 against 1,200, and so are sender name and send time. Each can still detect a difference of about 4–5 points. The costs are eight campaigns and segments instead of four, and the cross-effects become harder to read. The interaction between subject and sender name is already only a hint at this size.

**Decision needed: should send time be the third factor?**

- **Add send time (my pick):** half of batch 3 goes out at one time and half at another, for example 7 AM and 5 PM Pacific on the same weekday. We don't know where recipients live, so the answer is which Pacific time works for this mixed audience. That's the clock time we'd use for the remaining 3,600 people anyway. It costs four more campaigns and segments, which I'd build.
- **Keep two factors:** four groups, all at one time. Simpler, and send time stays untested.
- **Add language instead:** I'd only do this after checking whether production records each person's language or country. Without that, we'd be guessing who should get the translated email.

If we believe that a printer history is the most important factor, shouldn't we make sure that they are evenly distributed across the four splits so that we don't have a biased unbalanced data set coming back?

Yes, and the plan already does that. Before people are dealt into the four groups, they’re sorted by whether they own an Obico printer, whether they’re an early JusPrin user, and whether they use Gmail. Then each kind is dealt out evenly, so every group gets the same share of printer owners. A gap between groups can’t come from one group simply having more printer owners.

This is in the side chat. If this is what you plan to do, go ahead.

Going ahead with batch 3 as planned: four groups, deciding by subject and sender name, all sent at one time. I'll build the drafts with "JusPrin 2 is here" as a stand-in second subject, which you can edit before sending. I won't schedule or send anything to recipients.

content.text:
Yes, "JusPrin 2 is here" was my stand-in. When I proposed the test, the only reason I gave was that it was "a plainer one" than the current subject, and I said you'd choose the exact wording. So the result is real but narrow. It shows the stand-in beat "JusPrin 2: open source AI slicer, free with your own API key" (28.5% against 24.1% opened, unlikely to be chance). It doesn't show why, and it doesn't show the stand-in is a good subject. It only tells us the current one is worse.

The two subjects differ in several ways at once, so each of these is still only a hypothesis:

1. **Length.** The stand-in is 17 characters and the current one is 59. On a phone, the inbox list shows roughly the first 35–40 characters, so people saw "JusPrin 2: open source AI slicer, fr…". The cut hides the part meant to persuade.
2. **It reads like an ad.** "Free", "AI" and a feature pitch look like marketing. A short "X is here" looks like news from a product you already use. It could also change whether Gmail files the email under Promotions, but Gmail decides that mostly by sender, so I'd rank this low.
3. **"API key" puts people off.** To someone who has never made an API key, "free with your own API key" sounds like setup work, or like "not really free".
4. **It's news people half-expected.** Everyone in this batch used JusPrin 1, so "JusPrin 2 is here" answers something they already know about. If this is the reason, the lift should be biggest among early JusPrin 1 users and smallest among recent sign-ups.
5. **It sounds like a note from the maker.** The new subject gained 8 points from "Kenneth from JusPrin" and almost nothing from "Obi The Owl". A short subject with a person's name may read as a personal message. But this rests on one group of about 560 people, and our decision rule treats it as a hint only.

We can check hypothesis 4 with data we already have, at no cost. I'd split each group's openers by early versus newer JusPrin 1 users, and by printer owners, using the same hashed production data we balanced the groups with. I'd fold this into tomorrow's 48-hour read, which already planned to split by history. Hypotheses 1, 2, 3 and 5 can only be separated by new subjects.

**Proposal, not agreed:** don't send the winner to all of the roughly 3,600 people left. Instead, run one more round that pulls these explanations apart. All three versions would come from "Kenneth from JusPrin":
- "JusPrin 2 is here", as the baseline.
- A short subject with one benefit and no "free" or "API key", for example "JusPrin 2 is here: AI that fixes failed prints". If this beats the baseline, the pitch was never the problem; the length and the API-key wording were.
- A short, personal subject, for example "I rebuilt JusPrin". If this wins, the personal-note explanation gains ground.

Decision needed: should we spend the remaining people on a three-subject test, or send the winner to everyone? Three versions at about 1,200 each would use all 3,600 people. That leaves nobody to receive the final winner, but it can detect a gap of about 4–5 points, and later announcements to other lists would benefit. Sending "JusPrin 2 is here" to all 3,600 gets the best known version out now, but teaches us nothing more. A middle path is two versions at about 1,200 each, with the remaining 1,200 getting the winner. That middle path is my pick, because it keeps a real test and still sends the best subject to a third of the people. Which way do you want to go, and do you want to write the subjects yourself?
What were all the hypotheses that we were targeting batch 3 for? and come up with a clear conclusion on all of them. The conclusion can be validated, invalidated, or need further investigation.

## Re-check 2026-11-14 5:53 AM PST, and a refreshed explanation
Numbers now:
- Batch 1 (jusprin-support@), 23 hours after sending: 44 unique opens of 301 delivered (14.6%), 62 total opens, 1 unique click. Only 1 new opener since 10:34 PM, so it has levelled off. Gmail 36 of 242 (14.9%).
- Batch 2 (support@), 16 hours after sending: 45 unique opens of 199 delivered (22.6%), 52 total opens, 2 unique clicks, 2 unsubscribes. Gmail 40 of 171 (23.4%).
- Same-hour comparison now exists: at about 16 hours, batch 1 had 14.3% and batch 2 had 22.6%. Gmail: 14.5% vs 23.4%.
- Earlier campaigns' unique click rates for scale: 0.5% to 13%, most 2-3%. Batch 1 0.33%, batch 2 1.0%.

Who opened, joined with production (read-only, emails hashed in the page, never printed):
- Only 18 of the 547 JusPrin 1 users who chatted on or after Sep 19 have ever had an Obico printer (3%). So almost none of them get Obico's printer notification emails.
- Batch 1 printer owners opened 6 of 10 (60%) even from the new sender; everyone else 38 of 300 (12.7%). Batch 2 printer owners 0 of 6. Samples are tiny.
- Sign-up method made no difference (Google vs email: batch 1 14.5% vs 13.6%; batch 2 23.1% vs 20.3%). Joined over a year ago: batch 1 20% (11/55), batch 2 15% (4/26).
- For comparison, the JusPrin 1.4.0 email (Oct 2025, 41.6% opens) went to about 4,000 early JusPrin users; 896 of the 3,960 who had chatted before Oct 15 2025 had an Obico printer (23%).
- The 2026 campaigns with 44-56% opens (Re-Inventing TSD, Next-Gen AI) went to segments of the TSD list named "FD 2nd gen", i.e. Obico printer users.

Things that turned out NOT to be evidence:
- 309 of 310 batch 1 contacts and all 204 batch 2 contacts were created in SendGrid on Nov 12, 2026. But 35,454 of the TSD list's 47,307 contacts were also created then, and open history for the 2026 campaigns is almost entirely gone, so contacts were deleted and re-added at some point. This says nothing about whether these people got earlier Obico emails.

Outside reports (vendor blogs, not verified by us):
- Validity: Gmail image loading (which is how opens are counted) fell by about a third in late November 2025; Gmail began sorting Promotions by engagement in late 2025. Obico's own Gmail open rates stayed 42-46% in Feb and Apr 2026, so that change did not visibly hurt mail to Obico printer users.

Refreshed explanation (inference, not proven):
1. The sender address is a real cause. Same email, same hour: batch 2 from support@ is opened about 1.6 times as often as batch 1 from jusprin-support@, and the seed test put jusprin-support@ in Gmail Promotions.
2. The audience is the larger cause of the gap with earlier campaigns. Batches 1 and 2 go to people who almost never use Obico and so have little or no history of opening mail from obico.io. Earlier high-open campaigns went to Obico printer users, or (in Oct 2025) to early JusPrin users of whom about a quarter were Obico printer users, before Gmail's late-2025 changes. Even from the trusted sender, batch 2 is at 22.6%, well under the 33-56% earlier campaigns reached.

## Pool left for later batches (2026-11-14 ~6:30 AM PST)
- SendGrid TSD list: 6,784 JusPrin 1 contacts; 6,547 match the batch rules (opted in, not paid, no JusPrin 2 account, not dormant Pro); 6,033 of those have last chat on or before 09/18/2026 and have not been emailed. About 79% are Gmail.
- Only 8 of the 6,033 are contacts SendGrid created in Feb 2026, so "had a SendGrid contact since Feb 2026" cannot be used to split by email history (my earlier proposal; dropped).
- Production (read-only), JusPrin 1 users with last chat before 2026-09-19, 6,239 in all:
  - first chat before 2025-10-15 (so on the JusPrin list when the 1.3.0 and 1.4.0 emails went out): 3,895, of whom 889 have an Obico printer. Most of them last chatted in 2025 or earlier.
  - first chat after that: 2,344, of whom 143 have an Obico printer. Most last chatted in 2026.

## SendGrid vs Amazon SES (2026-11-14)
- obico.io already sends through Amazon SES (us-east-1): Obico server mail such as "We couldn't charge your Card" from admin@obico.io passes DKIM as obico.io and SPF through mail.obico.io. The obico.io SPF record includes amazonses.com. No List-Unsubscribe header on that mail (PR 1176 territory).
- Seed test: through SendGrid's shared IPs, support@ reached Gmail Primary 22/22, Yahoo inbox 8/8, AOL inbox 7/8. So SendGrid is not the Gmail/Yahoo/AOL problem.
- Open question: Hotmail/Outlook (5 spam, 8 missing of 13) and iCloud (3 of 3 missing) were the same for both senders, so the shared SendGrid IP is a candidate there. Real opens from Microsoft addresses: 2 of 33 (batch 1), 1 of 18 (batch 2); iCloud 0 of 4 (batch 1).
- 2026-11-14: Kenneth said "Not now" to a paid GlockApps month for an SES-vs-SendGrid seed test. No SES test is planned; Microsoft/iCloud placement stays an open question.

## Batch 3 plan: subject x sender name test (PROPOSAL, 2026-11-14; Kenneth asked for the plan, has not approved it; nothing built)
Design: 2x2 full factorial, four groups of about 600, all from support@obico.io, all sent the same minute, same body as batch 2.
| Group | Subject | Display name |
| b3a | current: "JusPrin 2: open source AI slicer, free with your own API key" | Obi The Owl (sender 3626841) |
| b3b | new subject (Kenneth picks the wording) | Obi The Owl |
| b3c | current | Kenneth from JusPrin (new sender, support@obico.io; to be created) |
| b3d | new subject | Kenneth from JusPrin |
Who: about 2,400 of the 6,033 eligible people not yet emailed (batch rules, last chat on or before 09/18/2026, jusprin2_sent is not t). The other ~3,600 later get the winning version.
Assignment: strata from production = Obico printer owner (yes/no) x first JusPrin 1 chat before 2025-10-15 (yes/no) x Gmail (yes/no). Within each stratum, order people by a salted SHA-256 of the email, take the first 40%, deal them to b3a, b3b, b3c, b3d in turn. Done inside the SendGrid page; production supplies only email hashes and strata.
Power: each factor compares about 1,200 with 1,200; detects about 4-5 points at open rates of 12-20% (80% power, 5% two-sided). The interaction (does the name only help with one subject) needs about twice that difference to show; treat it as a hint, not a result.
Measures: unique opens (all, and Gmail only) at 48 hours; unique clicks; JusPrin 2 accounts made within 7 days (production, read-only). History split read across all four groups (printer owners vs others, early vs newer users).
Decision rule, fixed before sending: for each factor, the version with more unique opens wins if the two-proportion test gives p < 0.05; otherwise there's no measured difference and Kenneth picks. If opens and JusPrin 2 sign-ups disagree, sign-ups decide.
Build steps once approved: production strata -> new text field jusprin2_arm on contacts (b3a..b3d) -> sender "Kenneth from JusPrin" <support@obico.io> -> four segments (batch rules + arm + jusprin2_sent is not t), counts checked against own counts -> four draft campaigns copied from batch 2 -> test sends of all four to k@obico.io -> Kenneth schedules all four for one time -> after sending, tag all four groups jusprin2_sent=t.

content.text:
I read batch 3 at about 47.5 hours after the send, which counts as the 48-hour read. That makes the 10:23 check redundant, so I cancelled it.

Batch 3 was built to test four hypotheses. Here's where each one landed:

1. **Subject line: confirmed.** "JusPrin 2 is here" got 31.0% of people to open, against 25.8% for the current subject. The gap is too large to be likely chance (p = 0.006), so by the rule we fixed before sending, it wins. Most of the gain came from people who started using JusPrin 1 early. Among newer users, the gain was small enough to be chance. That fits the idea that it works because people already knew JusPrin 2 was coming. That reading is still only a hint, not a result.

2. **Sender name: no measured difference.** "Kenneth from JusPrin" got 29.2% and "Obi The Owl" got 27.7%, which could easily be chance. Under our rule, that means you choose. There's one hint: with the new subject, your name did better (33.3% against 28.8%). That's not strong enough to count as a result.

3. **People with no history with obico.io open less: confirmed.** People with an Obico printer opened 37.8% of the time, against 24.4% for everyone else. People who joined JusPrin 1 early, and so got the old JusPrin 1.3 and 1.4 emails, opened no more than newer users. So it's the regular Obico printer emails that build the habit of opening mail from obico.io, not the old JusPrin emails. This is a correlation, not a random split. Printer owners may also be more engaged in general.

4. **Opens miss real readers: confirmed, but small.** 5 of the 32 people who clicked a link, and 2 of the 9 who made a JusPrin 2 account, never showed up as an open. So opens miss about 1 in 5 engaged readers. It shouldn't change any of the comparisons above. The email itself does drive sign-ups: 9 accounts from the 2,414 people emailed, and none from the 3,618 we held back (p < 0.001). Sign-ups are still too few to judge the subject or the sender by: 5 against 4. The Nov 21 read may add a few more.

One new finding: the weak step is clicking, not opening. About 28% opened but only 1.4% clicked a link, and that held for both subjects. Better subject lines won't fix that. The email body and its button are the next things to test.

The verdicts and per-campaign numbers are in `jusprin2-batch1-low-opens.md` in the shared notes folder. The 3,618 people not yet emailed should get "JusPrin 2 is here". Which sender name to use is the choice the box below asks you.
What are the other hypotheses that we can use to test with the remaining emails?

content.text:
With "JusPrin 2 is here" settled, the open rate is no longer the weak point. Clicking is. About 31% of people opened the new-subject version, but only 1.4% of all recipients clicked a link, and that was the same for both subjects. So I'd spend the remaining 3,618 people on hypotheses about the email body, not the subject.

These hypotheses come from reading the body as it was sent:

1. **There's no single clear thing to do.** The email has two plain links: the blog post, and the GitHub "latest release" page. That GitHub page is a list of files, and it's a hard place to land if you only want to install the app. My guess is that one clear "Download JusPrin 2" button would get more people to click.
2. **The pitch is abstract.** It opens with "AI works inside the project you have open", which doesn't say what problem it solves. The value you decided on for first run is that it fixes failed prints. My guess is that opening with a concrete case gets more clicks: a failed print, a photo, and the setting it changed. The first line also shows as preview text in the inbox, so this could move opens as well.
3. **The three ways to pay for AI read like homework.** Accounts, API keys and connecting Claude Code make it look complicated before anyone has tried it. This overlaps with the first two, so I'd fold it into the rewrite rather than test it separately.
4. **Your name only helps with the right subject.** This is last week's hint (33.3% against 28.8%, p = 0.11). Re-testing it would add little, because opens aren't the problem any more.
5. **Send day.** Batch 3 went out on a Saturday. A weekday send might do better, but I'd expect a small effect and wouldn't spend people on it.

Sign-ups can't be the measure. At 0.4%, all 3,618 people would yield only about 14 accounts, too few to compare anything. Clicks are the best signal we can measure. To spot clicks going from 1.4% to 2.8% takes about 1,650 people per version. A four-group test like batch 3 gives each factor about 1,800 against 1,800, which is just enough to test two of these at once.

Proposal (not agreed yet): send all 3,618 people "JusPrin 2 is here", with one sender name throughout, and four versions of the body:

| | Current opening | Failed-print opening |
|---|---|---|
| Two plain links (current) | about 900 | about 900 |
| One "Download" button, fewer options | about 900 | about 900 |

I'd measure clicks as the main result, opens to check the new first line, and JusPrin 2 sign-ups at 7 days as a rough check. Before sending, I'd draft both new pieces of text and get your edits on them.

Decision needed: should the remaining 3,618 people go into this body test, or all get the current email? The test gives every one of them the winning subject. Its cost is that about half of them get a weaker body, and it means one more round of drafting and building in SendGrid. In return, you learn whether the button or the opening drives clicks, and that carries over to the Obico list and later JusPrin emails. Sending everyone the current email costs nothing to set up, but we learn nothing more, and the 1.4% click rate stays a mystery. I'd run the test, because the click step is now where nearly all the people drop off. Should I draft the two new body versions?

content.text:
First, a correction. I pulled the email batch 3 actually sent out of SendGrid. It has no button and no images. The video, the download page and the announcement all appear as bare web addresses in the text. My earlier description of the links was off: there are three, not two. Your instinct is right, though: nothing in the email stands out as the thing to click.

**How I'd handle the remaining 3,618 people (a proposal, nothing built):**

- **Same for everyone:** the subject "JusPrin 2 is here", sent as "Kenneth from JusPrin" from support@obico.io, all at one time on a weekday morning, Pacific. Everyone also gets the rewritten pitch below, which I improved by judgement rather than testing, as you said.
- **The one test, about 1,809 people each.** Half get the download and announcement links as plain addresses, the way batch 3 had them. The other half get one large "Download JusPrin 2" button at the end, with "Read the announcement" as a small link under it. The wording and the download page are the same in both halves, so the button is the only difference.
- **Fair halves:** printer owners, early users and Gmail users are split evenly, as in batch 3.
- **What we measure:** clicks. Today 1.4% click. At this size we'd see it if the button lifts that to about 2.7%. JusPrin 2 sign-ups at 7 days are a rough second check.

**Draft of the shared text**

> **Preview line:** Show it a photo of a failed print, and it works out the fix.
>
> Hi [first name],
>
> You've used JusPrin 1, so I wanted you to hear it from me: JusPrin 2 is out.
>
> When a print fails, take a photo and show it to JusPrin 2. It works out what went wrong and which settings to change. You can also just tell it how you want a part printed, and it sets up the slice for you.
>
> Here's a short video of it: [video]
>
> It's free if you bring your own AI: an API key from Anthropic, OpenAI or OpenRouter, or an app you already use, like Claude Code or Codex. Or sign up in the app for 500 free credits, with no card needed. Your JusPrin 1 sign-in doesn't carry over, so that's a new account.
>
> JusPrin 2 replaces JusPrin 1 and brings over your printers and settings.
>
> [Download JusPrin 2, as a button or a plain address depending on the half]
> For Windows, Mac and Linux. [Read the announcement], with details and prices.
>
> If you have feedback or hit a bug, just reply to this email.
>
> Kenneth

What I changed and why:
- **Failed prints come first.** That's the value you chose for first run, and it's concrete. "You tell AI how you want to print something" is vaguer.
- **The AI options are cut from four lines to two sentences,** so they read as "it's free" instead of a setup guide.
- **The line about JusPrin's own AI being specialised in 3D printing is removed.** It isn't needed to get a click, and it makes a promise.

One thing worth fixing separately: both halves still send people to the GitHub releases page, which is a list of files. A page that picks the right download for the visitor's computer would likely help everyone. I've left it out so the button stays the only difference. If we changed both at once, we couldn't tell which one helped.

The plan is in the shared notes file, marked as a proposal.

Your clean sounds good, but this paragraph below is still confusing. 

[Download JusPrin 2, as a button or a plain address depending on the half]
For Windows, Mac and Linux. [Read the announcement], with details and prices.

The download CTA and the announcement CTA are mixed with the platform availability. Somehow it reads, it doesn't flow well for me. Do you have a good reason to phrase this CTA paragraph, which is arguably what paragraph this way?

No, I don't have a good reason. I carried that layout over from the earlier draft without questioning it. You're right that it squeezes three jobs into two lines: the download link, which platforms it runs on, and the announcement. A reader has to untangle which link does what.

Here's how I'd fix it. Each line does one job, and the platforms move up into the paragraph about the app.

> JusPrin 2 runs on Windows, Mac and Linux. It replaces JusPrin 1 and brings over your printers and settings.
>
> **[Download JusPrin 2]**
>
> Want the details and prices first? [Read the announcement].

The two halves of the test differ only in how the download line looks:

- **Button half:** "Download JusPrin 2" is a large button on its own line. "Read the announcement" is an ordinary text link underneath.
- **Plain half:** "Download JusPrin 2: [address]" on its own line, and "Want the details and prices first? Read the announcement: [address]" below it.

Why this order:
- **Platforms first:** someone deciding whether to click already knows it runs on their computer, so the button needs no caption.
- **Download second:** it's the action we want, so it comes right after the reasons to want the app.
- **Announcement last, as a question:** it's for people who aren't ready yet, so it reads as an alternative, not a second instruction.

Unless you'd rather change it, I'll use this when I build the drafts.

content.text:
So far the download button hasn't helped. Version A of batch 4 ended with a plain "Download JusPrin 2:" line and the GitHub address. Version B had a purple "Download JusPrin 2" button in its place. About 27 hours in, version A has slightly more clicks on every link, though only one of the gaps is bigger than chance would explain.

| | A: plain link | B: button | Could be chance? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Delivered | 1,691 | 1,665 | |
| Opened | 28.1% | 29.4% | yes (p = 0.44) |
| Clicked anything | 3.3% | 2.7% | yes (p = 0.30) |
| Clicked download | 27 (1.6%) | 18 (1.1%) | yes (p = 0.19) |
| Clicked the video | 50 | 39 | yes (p = 0.27) |
| Clicked the announcement | 19 (1.1%) | 6 (0.4%) | no (p = 0.01) |
| Unsubscribed | 1.8% | 1.1% | yes (p = 0.13) |
| Bounced | 1.4% | 3.0% | no (p = 0.002) |

The link counts are total clicks, so someone who clicked twice counts twice. That's the only per-link number SendGrid gives.

**What this suggests so far**
- **The button didn't raise downloads.** If anything it went the other way, but the gap is small enough to be chance.
- **The announcement lost clicks in the button version.** In version A it was a bare URL on its own line. In version B it was the short words "Read the announcement" in the sentence after the button. My guess is that the short inline link is easy to miss. That's a guess, not something this test measured.
- **The button version bounced twice as often: 52 against 25.** The two groups were split at random, so a gap this large is odd. One possible cause is that some mail servers reject the button's HTML. I haven't checked yet. Tomorrow I'll look at the bounce reasons for each version.

**The missed check**
The 11:49 job vanished without running even though the Mac was awake and the app was running. Tomorrow's 48-hour read at 11:53 AM uses the same kind of job, so it could be lost the same way. If you don't see a report from me by about noon, a one-line nudge will start it. That read saves batch 4's opens and clicks permanently and tells the rollout session it can delete the SendGrid contacts. SendGrid will also need to still be signed in.

I added these numbers to the shared note, `jusprin2-batch1-low-opens.md`.

Another Claude session sent a message:
<cross-session-message from="local_3e38de32-e8df-4f8c-b26d-1a20db4c0aca" from-name="Just Print V2 rollout plan">
All 48,401 SendGrid contacts were deleted today, Nov 17, on Kenneth's earlier yes. He asked to clear SendGrid now for the next batch, so this happened before your 48-hour read.

Before deleting, I saved batch 4's per-person opens and clicks, about 27 hours after the send, to /Users/kenneth/.claude/jusprin2-email-data/batch4_opens_clicks_2026-11-17.csv.
